title: Architecting a GTA-6 3D WebGL Portfolio: Deep Dive into Three.js, GSAP & Next.js 14
subtitle: How we rendered the neon streets of Vice City in the browser at 60 FPS
excerpt: A masterclass on combining Three.js custom procedural shaders, GLTF lighting rigs, and React 18 concurrent rendering to build an unforgettable cyber developer experience.
content:
## The Mission Objective

When standard developer portfolios feel like flat resumes, how do you capture a recruiter's attention in less than 3 seconds? You drop them straight into the sun-drenched, neon-drenched streets of Vice City.

In this technical breakdown, we explore how this portfolio was engineered from scratch using **Next.js 14 App Router**, **Three.js WebGL shaders**, and **GSAP smooth timeline orchestrations**.

```typescript
// Procedural Cyber Terrain Mesh Generator
const geometry = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(80, 80, 64, 64);
const material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
  color: 0x140124,
  wireframe: true,
  roughness: 0.2,
  metalness: 0.8,
});
```

### 1. Eliminating WebGL Frame Drops

The biggest enemy of browser 3D experiences is memory garbage collection. By utilizing custom instance buffers and reusing geometries across view changes, we achieved a consistent **60 FPS render cycle** even with CRT scanlines and dynamic point lighting enabled.

### 2. Audio Synthesis via Web Audio API

Instead of loading bulky 5MB audio files that slow down initial page loads, every sound effect—from the weapon wheel clicks to the iFruit dial tones—is generated procedurally in real-time via client-side oscillator frequency sweeps.

### 3. Dual-Layer Disk & Local Persistence

Changes made in the Admin Panel write directly to local JSON databases via server-side Node.js API handlers, while synchronizing with React state for zero-latency client feedback.
